title: Precision in Numbers: CV, SDI, Confidence Intervals, Geometric Mean and Detection Limits
summary: Learn to compare precision with the coefficient of variation, score proficiency results with the SDI, build and shrink a 95% confidence interval, summarize skewed lognormal data with the geometric mean, tell the limit of blank, limit of detection and limit of quantitation apart, and name the common interferences behind analytical specificity.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 10 Hits 9, 10, 11 and 14. Checked against Mishra 2019 (CV, mode, SEM), Kim 2021 and Kumar 2018 (SDI/z-score in EQA), Andreasson 2015 (SD and %CV per level; selectivity/specificity), Lee 2016 and Fay 2013 (confidence intervals, 1.96 and 2.575, quadrupling n halves the SEM), Motulsky 2025 (geometric mean of lognormal data), Armbruster 2008 (LoB/LoD/LoQ; abstract only), Dimeski 2008 (interferents; abstract only; both article bodies could not be retrieved: PMC captcha, Europe PMC 403) and 42 CFR 493.1253. Qualifications: Hit 11’s detection limit (“~3–4 × SD of ~10 zero-standard replicates”) is a blank-only rule, whereas Armbruster 2008 defines the LoD from the LoB plus replicates of a low-concentration sample (register flag rv-lod-traditional-vs-lob); Hit 11’s “response per unit analyte” meaning of analytic sensitivity is not taught. Hit 10 applies the geometric mean to “log-normal/skewed” data; Motulsky 2025 notes it can be a poor estimate of the median for skewed data that are not lognormal or contain outliers (register flag rv-geomean-lognormal-only). Not taught: the 25-OH vitamin D example figures (arithmetic 25.55 vs geometric 20.56 ng/mL, n = 12,434), the reviewer’s SDI worked numbers, the Gaussian table and figure.

objectives: Calculate a coefficient of variation and a standard deviation index, and say what each is used for.
Calculate a 95% confidence interval for a mean and predict how it changes with sample size.
Explain when and how to use the geometric mean, and define the mode.
Distinguish limit of blank, limit of detection and limit of quantitation, and name common interferences relevant to analytical specificity.

scenes.title: Three lines on a validation report
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a validation report for a new assay makes three claims. (1) QC level 1 has SD 2 at a mean of 100; level 2 has SD 4 at a mean of 300, “so level 2 is less precise”. (2) “To halve the width of our 95% confidence interval we will double the number of replicates.” (3) “Anything that reads above the mean of the blank counts as detected.” Question token: “Which claims survive?”

cues.text: A validation report for a new assay makes three claims. First: the high control has twice the standard deviation of the low one, so it must be less precise.
Second: doubling the number of replicates will halve the confidence interval. Third: anything that reads above the blank average counts as detected.
Which of these claims survive?

scenes.title: Spread and standing: CV and SDI
scenes.altText: CV card: coefficient of variation = 100 × SD ÷ mean, expressed as a percentage; an SD read without its mean can mislead. Worked example: SD 2 at mean 100 = CV 2%; SD 4 at mean 300 ≈ CV 1.3%. Method validations report imprecision as both SD and %CV at each level. SDI card: standard deviation index = (lab result − peer-group mean) ÷ peer-group SD, so it expresses bias as a multiple of the SD; external quality assessment results are scored by SDI or z-score. One scheme (KEQAS) treats SDI above 3 as unacceptable; schemes differ in their limits.

cues.text: A standard deviation means little without the mean beside it. The coefficient of variation fixes that: one hundred times the standard deviation divided by the mean, as a percentage.
So an SD of two at a mean of one hundred is a CV of two percent, while an SD of four at three hundred is only about one point three percent. Validation reports give both SD and CV at each level.
The standard deviation index scores a proficiency result: your result minus the peer-group mean, divided by the peer-group standard deviation. It states your bias as a number of standard deviations.
One Korean scheme counts an index above three as unacceptable, but external quality schemes set their limits differently.

scenes.title: Uncertainty and skew
scenes.altText: CI card: standard error of the mean = SD ÷ √n; a 95% confidence interval for a mean = mean ± 1.96 × SEM (z = 1.96 for 95%, 2.575 for 99%); for samples above about ten, the 95% CI spans about 2 SEM either side. Sample-size card: because n sits under a square root, quadrupling n is needed to halve the SEM; SEM and CI shrink with larger n, but the SD does not. Skew card: lognormal data have a long right tail; the arithmetic mean is the balance point of the whole distribution, tail included, and differs from the median; the geometric mean = antilog of the mean of the logarithms and equals the median of an ideal lognormal distribution. Mode token: the mode is the most frequent value; a data set can have more than one mode or none.

cues.text: The standard error of the mean is the standard deviation divided by the square root of n. A ninety-five percent confidence interval is the mean plus or minus one point nine six standard errors; for ninety-nine percent the multiplier is about two point five eight.
Because n sits under a square root, you need four times the sample to halve the standard error and the interval. The interval shrinks as n grows; the standard deviation does not.

Skewed data need another centre. Lognormal values have a long right tail, and the ordinary mean, the balance point of the whole distribution, no longer sits at the median. The geometric mean, the antilog of the mean of the logarithms, equals the median of an ideal lognormal distribution.
And the mode is simply the most frequent value; a data set can have several modes or none at all.

props.label: 4 × n → ½ SEM · SD does not shrink

scenes.title: Detecting a little, measuring the right thing
scenes.altText: Schematic ladder of low-end limits. Limit of blank (LoB) = mean of blank + 1.645 × SD of blank: the highest apparent result expected from a sample with no analyte. Limit of detection (LoD) = LoB + 1.645 × SD of a low-concentration sample: the lowest concentration reliably told apart from the LoB. Limit of quantitation (LoQ): the lowest level reliably detected and meeting predefined bias and imprecision goals; it may equal the LoD or be much higher. LoB uses blank replicates only; LoD also needs replicates of a low-concentration sample. Analytical specificity: US CLIA requires laboratories that modify or develop a test system to establish analytical specificity, to include interfering substances; haemolysis, icterus and lipaemia are the most frequently studied interferences, and drugs and antibodies can also interfere. Hook answer card.

cues.text: At the low end there is a ladder. The limit of blank is the blank mean plus one point six four five blank standard deviations. The limit of detection adds one point six four five standard deviations of a low-level sample. The limit of quantitation sits at or above it, where bias and imprecision goals are met.

Notice the difference. The limit of blank comes from blank replicates alone; the limit of detection also needs replicates of a sample known to hold a low concentration. The limit of quantitation may equal it or sit much higher.

Analytical specificity is about interference. US CLIA requires labs that modify or develop a test to establish it, including interfering substances. Haemolysis, icterus and lipaemia are the most studied; drugs and antibodies can interfere too.
Back to the hook: compare precision by CV, so level two is actually better; quadruple n to halve the interval; and set detection from the blank plus a low-level sample.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “The control with the larger SD is less precise” (✓ compare CVs; SD must be read against the mean); “Double n to halve the confidence interval” (✓ quadruple n, because SEM = SD ÷ √n); “Detection limit = blank mean + 2 SD” (✓ in the LoB/LoD approach, LoD = LoB + 1.645 SD of a low-concentration sample, so a low-level sample is needed).

cues.text: Trap one: the bigger standard deviation means worse precision. No: compare coefficients of variation, because the SD has to be read against its mean.
Trap two: double the sample to halve the confidence interval. No: the standard error divides by the square root of n, so you need four times the sample.

Trap three: the detection limit is just the blank mean plus two SD. No: in the blank and low-sample approach, the limit of detection is the limit of blank plus one point six four five SD of a low-level sample.

props.title: ✗ “LoD = blank mean + 2 SD.”
lines: ✓ LoB, then LoD = LoB + 1.645 SD (low sample)

scenes.title: Divide, quadruple, log, climb
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Divide by the MEAN to compare, by the SD to score. FOUR times the people for HALF the doubt. LOG the long tail. Climb Blank → Low → Quantify.” Tokens: CV compares · SDI scores; 4 × n = ½ CI; log the tail; LoB → LoD → LoQ. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: divide by the mean to compare, by the SD to score. Four times the people for half the doubt. Log the long tail. And climb from blank, to low, to quantify.

Where it breaks: proficiency schemes set different pass limits; the two standard error shortcut needs more than about ten values; and the geometric mean misleads when data are skewed but not lognormal, or contain outliers.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “CV = 100 × SD ÷ mean · SDI = (lab − peer mean) ÷ peer SD”, “95% CI = mean ± 1.96 SEM (4 × n halves it) · geomean for lognormal · LoB → LoD → LoQ”.

cues.text: Compare precision with the coefficient of variation, score proficiency results with the standard deviation index, quadruple the sample size to halve a confidence interval, summarize lognormal data with the geometric mean, and set detection limits from blank and low-level samples rather than from the blank alone.

props.label: CV = 100 × SD ÷ mean · SDI = (lab − peer mean) ÷ peer SD
CI = mean ± 1.96 SEM (4 × n halves it) · geomean · LoB → LoD → LoQ

explanation.what: Plain language: a spread number means little until you set it against the size of the result; a proficiency score says how many spreads you sit from your peers; a confidence interval says how precisely you know an average, and it narrows only slowly as you add samples; long-tailed data are better summarized on a log scale; and “detected” has to be defined against blank and low-level samples, with interferences checked separately. Scientific terms: standard deviation (SD), coefficient of variation (CV), standard deviation index (SDI), z-score, external quality assessment (EQA) / proficiency testing (PT), standard error of the mean (SEM), confidence interval (CI), lognormal distribution, geometric mean, median, mode, limit of blank (LoB), limit of detection (LoD), limit of quantitation (LoQ), analytical sensitivity, analytical specificity, selectivity, interference.
explanation.why: The CV removes the scale of the mean so imprecision can be compared across levels. The SDI divides the difference from the peer mean by the peer SD, so bias reads as a multiple of the SD. The SEM divides the SD by √n, so precision of the mean improves with the square root of the sample size. A long right tail pulls the arithmetic mean (the balance point) upward, whereas the geometric mean of lognormal data sits at the median. The LoB describes only what blanks produce; the LoD is the lowest concentration reliably distinguished from the LoB, so it is determined with replicates of a low-concentration sample as well.
explanation.measure: CV = 100 × SD ÷ mean (%). SDI = (lab result − peer mean) ÷ peer SD; one scheme (KEQAS) treats SDI > 3 as unacceptable. SEM = SD ÷ √n; 95% CI = mean ± 1.96 × SEM (99%: z = 2.575); quadrupling n halves the SEM. Geometric mean = antilog of the mean of the logs (equivalently the n-th root of the product). LoB = mean(blank) + 1.645 SD(blank); LoD = LoB + 1.645 SD(low sample); LoQ ≥ LoD (it may equal the LoD or be much higher).
explanation.differs: SD (absolute spread) vs CV (relative spread); SDI (bias against peers) vs CV (imprecision); SD (does not shrink with n) vs SEM/CI (shrink with n); arithmetic vs geometric mean; mean vs median vs mode; LoB vs LoD vs LoQ; selectivity (a graded property, the recommended term) vs specificity (an absolute one), terms often used interchangeably.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate a CV or SDI, pick the sample size that halves a CI, recall z = 1.96 for a 95% CI, choose the geometric mean for lognormal data, define the mode, or order LoB, LoD and LoQ.

takeaway: Compare precision with the coefficient of variation, score proficiency results with the standard deviation index, quadruple the sample size to halve a confidence interval, summarize lognormal data with the geometric mean, and set detection limits from blank and low-level samples rather than from the blank alone.

questions.stem: In a proficiency-testing event, your laboratory reports 96 mg/dL. The peer-group mean is 100 mg/dL with a peer-group SD of 2 mg/dL. What is your standard deviation index?

options.rationale: Correct. SDI = (96 − 100) ÷ 2 = −2.0: the result sits two peer SDs below the peer mean.
Incorrect. The result is below the peer mean, so the SDI is negative.
Incorrect. That is the raw difference in mg/dL; it must be divided by the peer SD.
Incorrect. That is a CV-style ratio (SD ÷ mean × 100), not an SDI; the SDI has no units.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for a mean was calculated from 25 replicates. With the SD unchanged, how many replicates are needed to make the interval half as wide?

options.rationale: Correct. The width depends on SD ÷ √n, so quadrupling n (25 → 100) doubles √n and halves the interval.
Incorrect. Doubling n does not double √n, so the interval narrows by less than half.
Incorrect. That is 25 squared, far more replicates than needed to halve the width.

options.text: No number, because the SD does not change with n
options.rationale: Incorrect. The SD does not shrink with n, but the SEM and the confidence interval do.

questions.stem: An analyte’s results in healthy people are right-skewed and lognormal. Which statement about summarizing their centre is correct?

options.text: The geometric mean, the antilog of the mean of the logged values, estimates the median
options.rationale: Correct. For an ideal lognormal distribution the geometric mean equals the median, and it is the standard way to quantify the centre of a lognormal distribution.

options.text: The arithmetic mean is best because it uses every value equally
options.rationale: Incorrect. The arithmetic mean is the balance point of the whole distribution, long right tail included, so for lognormal data it does not sit at the median.

options.text: The mode, because it is always unique
options.rationale: Incorrect. The mode is the most frequent value, and a data set can have several modes or none.

options.text: Mean ± 1.96 SD of the raw values
options.rationale: Incorrect. That describes a spread around the arithmetic mean, not the centre of the data.

references.citation: Mishra P, Pandey CM, Singh U, Gupta A, Sahu C, Keshri A. Descriptive statistics and normality tests for statistical data. Ann Card Anaesth. 2019;22(1):67-72. doi:10.4103/aca.aca_157_18
references.usedFor: CV = 100 × (SD ÷ mean), expressed as %, because SD read without the mean can mislead; mode = most frequent value, with possibly several or no modes; standard error = sample SD ÷ √n.

references.citation: Kim S, Lee K, Park HD, Lee YW, Chun S, Min WK. Schemes and Performance Evaluation Criteria of Korean Association of External Quality Assessment (KEQAS) for Improving Laboratory Testing. Ann Lab Med. 2021;41(2):230-239. doi:10.3343/alm.2021.41.2.230
references.usedFor: SDI = (laboratory result − peer-group mean) ÷ peer-group SD, reflecting bias as a multiple of the SD; SDI > 3 unacceptable in KEQAS; EQA schemes use different performance criteria (SDI/z-score limits or fixed limits).

references.citation: Kumar BV, Mohan T. Sigma metrics as a tool for evaluating the performance of internal quality control in a clinical chemistry laboratory. J Lab Physicians. 2018;10(2):194-199. doi:10.4103/jlp.jlp_102_17
references.usedFor: External quality control is interpreted by Z-score or standard deviation index; a Z-score states how many SDs a result lies from the expected mean.

references.citation: Andreasson U, Perret-Liaudet A, van Waalwijk van Doorn LJ, et al. A Practical Guide to Immunoassay Method Validation. Front Neurol. 2015;6:179. doi:10.3389/fneur.2015.00179
references.usedFor: Full text via Europe PMC. Imprecision is reported as both SD and %CV at each level; selectivity = ability to measure and differentiate the analyte in the presence of components that may be expected to be present; selectivity and specificity are often used interchangeably, selectivity (graded) being the recommended term over specificity (absolute); its LLOQ procedure uses 16 blanks and a signal 10 SD above the blank mean (used for register flag rv-lod-traditional-vs-lob as evidence that blank-based limits are method-dependent).

references.citation: Lee DK. Alternatives to P value: confidence interval and effect size. Korean J Anesthesiol. 2016;69(6):555-562. doi:10.4097/kjae.2016.69.6.555
references.usedFor: CI for a population mean = mean ± z × SEM for normally distributed data; correct interpretation (95% of intervals from repeated samples include the population mean); CIs narrow as sample size increases.

references.citation: Fay DS, Gerow K. A biologist's guide to statistical thinking and analysis. WormBook. 2013:1-54. doi:10.1895/wormbook.1.159.1
references.usedFor: z = 1.96 for a 95% CI and 2.575 for 99%; for samples above about ten a 95% CI spans about two SEMs either side of the mean; a quadrupling of sample size is required to halve the SEM; SE and CI shrink with larger samples, the SD does not.

references.citation: Motulsky HJ, Head T, Clarke PBS. Analyzing lognormal data: A nonmathematical practical guide. Pharmacol Rev. 2025;77(3):100049. doi:10.1016/j.pharmr.2025.100049
references.usedFor: Lognormal data have a positive skew (long right tail); the arithmetic mean is the balance point and differs from the median; geometric mean = antilog of the mean of the logs (or n-th root of the product), equal to the median of an ideal lognormal distribution and the standard way to give its centre; it can be a poor estimate of the median when skewed data are not lognormal or contain outliers.

references.citation: Armbruster DA, Pry T. Limit of blank, limit of detection and limit of quantitation. Clin Biochem Rev. 2008;29(Suppl 1):S49-S52.
references.usedFor: Abstract (Summary) only: the article body is a PDF behind a captcha (PMC) / HTTP 403 (Europe PMC), and NCBI efetch returns only the Summary; an earlier page-fetch tool summary was not relied on. From the Summary: LoB = highest apparent concentration expected from blank replicates = mean blank + 1.645 SD(blank); LoD = lowest concentration likely to be reliably distinguished from the LoB, determined from the LoB and replicates of a low-concentration sample, LoD = LoB + 1.645 SD(low-concentration sample); LoQ = lowest concentration reliably detected and meeting predefined bias and imprecision goals, equal to the LoD or much higher.

references.citation: Dimeski G. Interference testing. Clin Biochem Rev. 2008;29(Suppl 1):S43-S48.
references.usedFor: Abstract (Summary) only: the article body is a PDF not retrievable here (PMC captcha, Europe PMC 403); NCBI efetch returns only the Summary. From the Summary: interference occurs when a substance or process falsely alters an assay result; endogenous or exogenous; haemolysis, icterus and lipaemia are the most frequently studied; drug interference (parent drug, metabolites or additives); immunoassay interference most commonly from antibodies.

references.citation: 42 CFR § 493.1253 — Standard: Establishment and verification of performance specifications (eCFR, version current to 2026-10-01).
references.usedFor: Regulation text via the eCFR API (2026-10-01). Laboratories that modify an FDA-cleared or approved test system, introduce one not subject to FDA clearance, or use one without manufacturer specifications must establish accuracy, precision, analytical sensitivity, analytical specificity to include interfering substances, reportable range and reference intervals.

claims.text: CV formula and purpose; SD and %CV reported per level; SDI formula, meaning and use in EQA/PT; scheme-dependent limits.
SEM = SD ÷ √n; 95% CI = mean ± 1.96 SEM (99%: 2.575); about 2 SEM for n above about ten; quadrupling n halves the SEM; SD does not shrink with n; CI interpretation.
Lognormal right skew; geometric mean as antilog of mean of logs and median of lognormal data; its limits for non-lognormal or outlier-laden data; mode definition.
LoB, LoD and LoQ definitions and formulas; LoD needs a low-concentration sample as well as blanks; LoQ may equal or exceed the LoD.

Analytical specificity to include interfering substances (CLIA, for labs that modify or develop test systems); haemolysis, icterus and lipaemia are the most studied interferences, with drugs and antibodies also interfering; selectivity vs specificity terminology.

25-OH vitamin D arithmetic vs geometric mean figures (25.55 vs 20.56 ng/mL, n = 12,434); the reviewer’s “~3–4 × SD of ~10 zero-standard replicates” rule; the claim that a blank-only limit (mean + 2 SD of about 20 blanks) shows only the ability to measure nothing; use of “analytical sensitivity” for the calibration slope and whether it is a synonym for LoD; replicate numbers for establishing or verifying an LoD; cross-reacting substances as interferents.
claims.note: Not taught. The vitamin D dataset was not located in an open source; the remaining points appear only in the body of Armbruster 2008 and Dimeski 2008, whose own text could not be retrieved (abstracts only).

claims.text: Scenario and QC numbers invented; limit ladder and distributions schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 10 Hit 11 gives the detection limit as “~3–4 × SD of ~10 zero-standard replicates”, a blank-only rule. Armbruster 2008 (Summary) defines LoB = mean(blank) + 1.645 SD(blank) and the LoD as the lowest concentration reliably distinguished from the LoB, determined with a low-concentration sample: LoD = LoB + 1.645 SD(low sample). Blank-based multipliers vary by method (Andreasson 2015 uses 16 blanks and 10 SD for an LLOQ). The lesson teaches the LoB/LoD/LoQ definitions and not the reviewer’s replicate rule (register flag rv-lod-traditional-vs-lob).

Ch. 10 Hit 10 recommends the geometric mean for “log-normal/skewed” data. Motulsky 2025 supports it for lognormal data but notes it can be a poor estimate of the median for skewed data that are not lognormal or contain outliers (register flag rv-geomean-lognormal-only).

The performance-specification list (analytical sensitivity, analytical specificity including interfering substances) is quoted from US CLIA (42 CFR 493.1253). Philippine laboratory requirements are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local rules.
